docs.title: API Mastery Path
docs.text:
Learn API Engineering progressively through foundations, capabilities, framework implementations, projects, and production systems.

The goal of this site is not merely to learn how to create endpoints.

The goal is to progressively develop API Engineering mastery through deliberate practice, realistic scenarios, framework implementations, and production-oriented thinking.

docs.title: Learning Progression
docs.text:
Fundamentals
    ↓
Capabilities
    ↓
Implementations
    ↓
Projects
    ↓
Production APIs

This progression is reflected throughout the site:

Fundamentals
    ↓
Capabilities
    ↓
FastAPI Implementations
    ↓
Projects
    ↓
Production APIs

Each level builds upon the understanding developed in the previous level.

docs.title: 1. Fundamentals
docs.text:
Build a strong understanding of how APIs work.

Topics include:

  • HTTP
  • REST
  • JSON
  • Content Types
  • Cookies vs Tokens
  • OpenAPI

These pages focus on the concepts that underpin all APIs regardless of framework or programming language.

Goal: Learn how APIs work.

docs.title: 2. Capabilities
docs.text:
Develop practical API Engineering thinking through common API capabilities.

Topics include:

  • Routing
  • Validation
  • Error Handling
  • Documentation
  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Filtering
  • Pagination
  • Versioning
  • Testing

Capability pages focus on problems, reasoning, design, and tradeoffs.

They answer questions such as:

  • Why does this capability exist?
  • What problem does it solve?
  • When should it be used?
  • What makes a good solution?

Frameworks are intentionally not the focus.

Goal: Learn how APIs solve problems.

docs.title: 3. FastAPI Implementations
docs.text:
Learn how FastAPI implements API capabilities.

Topics include:

  • FastAPI Routing
  • FastAPI Validation
  • FastAPI Error Handling
  • FastAPI Documentation
  • FastAPI Authentication
  • FastAPI Authorization
  • FastAPI Filtering
  • FastAPI Pagination
  • FastAPI Versioning
  • FastAPI Testing

Implementation pages focus on:

  • framework tools
  • framework patterns
  • coding exercises
  • reusable solutions

Each implementation page is designed to follow its corresponding capability page.

Goal: Learn how FastAPI implements API concepts.

docs.title: 4. Projects
docs.text:
Combine multiple capabilities into realistic APIs.

Examples include:

  • Notes API
  • Task API
  • URL Shortener
  • Knowledge Base API

Projects bridge the gap between isolated capabilities and complete API systems.

They demonstrate how capabilities work together in realistic applications.

Goal: Learn how API capabilities compose into systems.

docs.title: 5. Production APIs
docs.text:
Learn how APIs operate in real-world environments.

Topics include:

  • Logging
  • Monitoring
  • Observability
  • Security
  • Deployment
  • Containers
  • Reverse Proxies
  • Scaling

Building an API is only part of API Engineering.

Production APIs must also be deployed, monitored, secured, and maintained.

Goal: Learn how APIs survive in production.

docs.title: Who Is This For?
docs.text:
This site is designed for:

  • Developers preparing for professional API work
  • Anyone interested in long-term API Engineering mastery

docs.title: Exercise Philosophy
docs.text:
Exercises begin with realistic problems rather than framework syntax.

The goal is not merely to learn API tooling.

The goal is to understand:

  • Why a capability exists
  • When a capability becomes necessary
  • How APIs solve practical problems
  • How frameworks implement those solutions

For this reason, capability exercises begin with scenarios rather than code.

Instead of:

Add a query parameter.

an exercise might begin with:

Your API now contains hundreds of thousands of records
and consumers cannot find the data they need.

The intention is to help learners think:

"I've encountered that problem before."

rather than:

"Here's another tutorial."

Every exercise is designed to reinforce API Engineering thinking through realistic situations.

This site exists to support that journey.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication is the capability of verifying the identity of a caller.

When an API receives a request, it must often answer a simple but important question:

Who is making this request?

Authentication exists to provide a reliable way to answer that question.

Without authentication, systems cannot determine whether requests originate from trusted users, applications, or services.

Authentication is one of the foundational security capabilities of modern APIs.

Professional API engineers need to understand authentication because most real-world APIs protect data, functionality, or resources that should not be accessible to everyone.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine a Payroll API that supports the following endpoint:

GET /employees/payroll

The endpoint returns salary information for employees.

The API works.

The endpoint returns correct data.

However, there is a problem.

Anyone who discovers the endpoint can access payroll information.

The API has no way of determining:

  • Who is making the request
  • Whether the caller is a legitimate employee
  • Whether the caller should be trusted

The issue is not routing.

The issue is not validation.

The issue is identity.

Authentication exists because APIs often need to verify who is making a request before providing access to protected functionality.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
Authentication allows systems to make decisions based on verified identities.

Without authentication, APIs cannot distinguish trusted callers from unknown callers.

docs.title: Maintainability
docs.text:
Consistent authentication approaches simplify API development and maintenance.

Teams can apply the same authentication strategy across many endpoints and services.

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text:
Consumers should interact with authentication mechanisms in predictable ways.

Consistent authentication flows improve usability and reduce confusion.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Authentication is one of the primary security controls used by APIs.

It helps protect:

  • Sensitive data
  • Private resources
  • Administrative functionality
  • Organizational systems

Without authentication, APIs often become vulnerable to unauthorized access.

docs.title: User Experience
docs.text:
Well-designed authentication helps legitimate users access APIs successfully while preventing unauthorized access.

The goal is to provide security without unnecessary friction.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Identity answers the question:

Who are you?

Authentication exists to establish identity.

An identity may represent:

  • A person
  • An application
  • A service
  • A device

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Credentials are evidence used to prove identity.

Examples include:

  • Passwords
  • API keys
  • Tokens
  • Certificates

The specific credential type matters less than the underlying goal:

Prove identity.

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorization
docs.text:
These concepts are closely related but distinct.

Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Authorization answers:

What are you allowed to do?

Authentication typically happens first.

Authorization decisions often depend on authenticated identity.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A session allows a system to remember an authenticated user between requests.

After successful authentication, the system can recognize future requests without requiring the user to repeatedly prove their identity.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
A token is a credential that can be presented with requests.

Tokens are commonly used in modern APIs because they allow identity information to travel with requests.

docs.title: Trust
docs.text:
Authentication is fundamentally about trust.

A system receives a request and must decide:

Can I trust the identity being presented?

Authentication provides mechanisms for establishing that trust.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A company creates an API that allows users to delete customer records.

The endpoint is publicly accessible:

DELETE /customers/42

No authentication is required.

Anyone who knows the endpoint can submit requests.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why authentication exists.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Explain the problem authentication solves
  • Identify risks associated with unauthenticated APIs
  • Describe why identity matters

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think about who might discover the endpoint.

Stronger Hint

Consider what prevents unauthorized users from submitting requests.

Almost There

The API currently has no way to verify who is making the request.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The API cannot determine who is making requests.

Because identity cannot be verified, unauthorized users may gain access to protected functionality.

Authentication exists to establish trust and verify identity before protected operations are performed.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Authentication becomes easier to understand when viewed as a solution to a real problem.

The problem is not technology.

The problem is determining who should be trusted.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: A team operates three APIs:

docs.title: Public Weather API
docs.text: Provides public weather forecasts.

docs.title: Employee Payroll API
docs.text: Provides payroll information.

docs.title: Administrative Dashboard API
docs.text:
Allows system configuration.

The team must decide where authentication is required.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Apply authentication concepts to API design decisions.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Identify when authentication is appropriate
  • Evaluate security requirements
  • Explain authentication decisions

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Not every API requires the same level of protection.

Stronger Hint

Consider the sensitivity of the information being exposed.

Almost There

The more sensitive the data or functionality, the more likely authentication is needed.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

A possible approach:

  • Public Weather API: Authentication may not be required.
  • Employee Payroll API: Authentication should be required.
  • Administrative Dashboard API: Authentication should be required.

Authentication decisions are often driven by risk and sensitivity.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: API engineers must make practical decisions about when authentication is necessary and why.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing a Task Management API.

Features include:

  • Creating tasks
  • Updating tasks
  • Deleting tasks
  • Viewing personal tasks

Multiple users will use the API.

Each user should access only their own information.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Design an authentication strategy.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Identify authentication requirements
  • Explain how identities affect API behavior
  • Design a coherent authentication approach

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think about how the API identifies users.

Stronger Hint

The API must know which user is making each request.

Almost There

User-specific functionality typically requires authenticated identities.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The API should require users to authenticate before accessing personal task data.

Once authenticated, the API can associate requests with individual identities.

This enables the API to provide personalized and secure behavior.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Real-world APIs often combine authentication with data ownership and access control concerns.

Authentication is a foundational building block for these systems.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your organization operates dozens of APIs.

Each team implements authentication differently.

Some use API keys.

Some use tokens.

Some use custom solutions.

Developers struggle because every API behaves differently.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify reusable authentication patterns.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Recognize authentication inconsistencies
  • Identify opportunities for standardization
  • Think about authentication at organizational scale
  • Explain the benefits of common approaches

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Consistency is valuable for both developers and consumers.

Stronger Hint

Reusable standards reduce complexity.

Almost There

Authentication strategies become easier to maintain when teams follow shared patterns.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

An organization may establish authentication standards covering:

  • Credential types
  • Identity verification processes
  • Token handling
  • Security expectations

Shared standards improve consistency and reduce duplication across teams.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Professional API engineers often help establish security patterns that scale across many systems.

Authentication is most effective when approached consistently.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Authentication solves the problem of verifying identity.

Without authentication:

  • APIs cannot reliably determine who is making requests
  • Sensitive functionality becomes difficult to protect
  • Trust becomes difficult to establish
  • Security risks increase

Professional API engineers rely on authentication to build secure and trustworthy systems.

Authentication provides a foundation for:

  • Security
  • Trust
  • Access control
  • User-specific experiences
  • Protected resources

Before an API can decide what a caller is allowed to do, it must first determine who the caller is.

Authentication is how that identity is established.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Authorization is the capability of determining what an authenticated identity is allowed to do.

Once an API knows who is making a request, it must often answer a second question:

What is this caller allowed to do?

Authorization exists to answer that question.

Most real-world systems contain functionality that should not be available to every user.

Examples include:

  • Administrative actions
  • Sensitive data
  • Financial information
  • Internal resources
  • User-specific content

Professional API engineers need to understand authorization because verifying identity alone is not enough to protect systems.

Authentication establishes who a caller is.

Authorization determines what they can access.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine an API used by a company.

Employees can access:

GET /employees/profile

Managers can access:

GET /employees/payroll

System administrators can access:

DELETE /employees/42

The API already supports authentication.

Every caller must sign in before using the API.

However, a problem remains.

An authenticated employee could attempt to access payroll information or delete employee records.

The API knows who the user is.

But it does not yet know what they should be allowed to do.

Authorization exists because authenticated users often have different levels of access.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
Authorization ensures requests are handled according to defined access rules.

Systems behave more predictably when permissions are enforced consistently.

docs.title: Maintainability
docs.text:
Well-designed authorization models make it easier to manage access as systems grow.

Permissions can evolve without redesigning entire APIs.

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text:
Users and applications should encounter the same authorization rules regardless of which endpoint they access.

Consistent enforcement improves trust and predictability.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Authorization protects:

  • Sensitive data
  • Administrative functions
  • Internal operations
  • User-specific resources

Without authorization, authenticated users may gain inappropriate access.

docs.title: User Experience
docs.text:
Good authorization helps users access the resources they need while preventing access to resources they should not use.

The goal is protection without unnecessary confusion.

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorization
docs.text:
These concepts are related but different.

Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Authorization answers:

What are you allowed to do?

Authorization typically depends on successful authentication.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions define specific actions that are allowed.

Examples:

Create User
Delete User
View Reports
Manage Billing

Permissions often represent business capabilities.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Roles group permissions together.

Examples:

Employee
Manager
Administrator

Roles simplify permission management.

Instead of assigning individual permissions to every user, permissions can be assigned to roles.

docs.title: Resource Ownership
docs.text:
Many APIs allow users to access resources they own.

Examples:

My Tasks
My Orders
My Documents

Ownership is a common authorization strategy.

A user may be authenticated but still restricted from viewing another user's resources.

docs.title: Principle of Least Privilege
docs.text:
Users should have only the access necessary to perform their tasks.

Example:

Read access

should not automatically imply:

Delete access

Limiting permissions reduces risk.

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
Access control refers to the rules used to determine whether actions should be allowed.

Authorization is ultimately about enforcing access control decisions.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A company provides an API for customer management.

The API requires authentication.

Every employee can log in successfully.

The API also allows customer deletion:

DELETE /customers/42

No additional access checks exist.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why authorization exists.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Explain the difference between authentication and authorization
  • Identify authorization risks
  • Describe why identity alone is insufficient

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

The API knows who the user is.

Stronger Hint

Ask whether every authenticated user should have identical access.

Almost There

Authentication proves identity. Authorization determines permissions.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Authentication confirms the user's identity.

Authorization determines whether that identity should be allowed to perform a specific action.

Without authorization, authenticated users may gain access to functionality that should remain restricted.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
A common misconception is that authentication alone protects an API.

Real systems often require additional authorization decisions after identity has been established.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A team is designing access rules for an internal API.

Users belong to one of three roles:

Employee
Manager
Administrator

The API supports:

View Personal Profile
View Payroll Data
Delete Employee Records

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Apply authorization concepts to API design.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Match permissions to roles
  • Explain authorization decisions
  • Recognize access control requirements

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Some actions are more sensitive than others.

Stronger Hint

Consider which role genuinely needs each capability.

Almost There

Permissions should align with responsibilities.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

One possible approach:

  • Employee → View Personal Profile
  • Manager → View Personal Profile, View Payroll Data
  • Administrator → View Personal Profile, View Payroll Data, Delete Employee Records

Authorization decisions should follow business requirements and security needs.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
API engineers frequently design role-based access systems.

Understanding how permissions map to responsibilities is an important skill.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing a Task Management API.

Each user can:

  • Create tasks
  • View their own tasks
  • Update their own tasks

Administrators can:

  • View all tasks
  • Delete any task

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Design a complete authorization strategy.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Define access rules
  • Distinguish ownership from administrative access
  • Combine multiple authorization concepts

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Not every authorization rule requires roles.

Stronger Hint

Ownership can be a form of authorization.

Almost There

Consider how users and administrators should differ.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The API could use a combination of ownership and role-based authorization.

Users:

  • Create tasks
  • View their own tasks
  • Update their own tasks

Administrators:

  • Access all tasks
  • Delete any task

Combining authorization strategies often creates more flexible systems.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Real-world APIs frequently require multiple authorization approaches working together.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your organization operates dozens of APIs.

Each team creates authorization rules independently.

Some use roles.

Some use permissions.

Some use custom solutions.

Developers struggle because authorization behaves differently across systems.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify reusable authorization patterns.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Recognize authorization inconsistencies
  • Identify common patterns
  • Think about authorization across many systems
  • Explain the value of standardization

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think beyond a single API.

Stronger Hint

Shared authorization models reduce complexity.

Almost There

Consistent authorization approaches are easier to maintain and understand.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

An organization may standardize:

  • Role definitions
  • Permission naming
  • Access review processes
  • Authorization strategies

Shared standards help create predictable and maintainable systems.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Professional API engineers often contribute to security and access standards that extend beyond individual APIs.

Authorization becomes more valuable when handled consistently.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Authorization solves the problem of controlling access after identity has been established.

Without authorization:

  • Authenticated users may gain excessive access
  • Sensitive data may be exposed
  • Administrative functionality may be misused
  • Security risks increase

Professional API engineers use authorization to enforce business rules and protect resources.

Authorization helps provide:

  • Access control
  • Data protection
  • Security
  • Consistency
  • Trust

Authentication determines who a caller is.

Authorization determines what that caller is allowed to do.

Together, they form a foundational part of secure API design.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Documentation is the capability of communicating how an API should be used.

An API may function perfectly from a technical perspective, yet still be difficult to understand, adopt, and maintain if consumers do not know:

  • What endpoints exist
  • What inputs are required
  • What responses are returned
  • How authentication works
  • What errors can occur

Documentation exists because APIs are not used only by machines.

They are used by people.

Good documentation helps developers discover, understand, and successfully integrate with APIs.

As APIs grow in complexity and are used by more teams, documentation becomes an essential part of the API itself.

Professional API engineers treat documentation as part of the product rather than something added later.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine joining a new team.

You are asked to integrate with an existing User API.

You are given only a base URL:

https://api.example.com

Nobody can answer:

  • Which endpoints exist
  • Which fields are required
  • Which fields are optional
  • What authentication method is used
  • What errors might be returned

The API technically works.

But it is difficult to consume.

Developers spend hours reading source code, asking questions, and experimenting with requests.

The problem is not functionality.

The problem is communication.

Documentation exists because APIs need to communicate their capabilities, expectations, and contracts to consumers.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
Documentation helps consumers use APIs correctly.

Fewer misunderstandings often result in fewer incorrect requests and integration problems.

docs.title: Maintainability
docs.text:
Well-documented APIs are easier to support over time.

Future developers can understand the API without relying entirely on previous team members.

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text:
Documentation helps establish shared expectations.

Consumers can learn one style of documentation and apply it throughout an API ecosystem.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Documentation explains:

  • Authentication requirements
  • Authorization expectations
  • Security considerations

Without documentation, consumers may misuse APIs or create insecure integrations.

docs.title: User Experience
docs.text:
Developers are users too.

A well-documented API is often perceived as easier, cleaner, and more professional.

Good documentation improves developer experience.

docs.title: API Consumers
docs.text:
Documentation is written for API consumers.

Examples include:

  • Frontend developers
  • Mobile developers
  • Other backend services
  • External partners
  • Future team members
  • Future you

Understanding the audience helps determine what information should be documented.

docs.title: API Contracts
docs.text:
An API contract describes:

  • Available operations
  • Expected inputs
  • Expected outputs
  • Rules and constraints

Documentation communicates this contract.

Consumers rely on the contract to build applications.

docs.title: Discoverability
docs.text:
A discoverable API helps consumers answer questions such as:

What can this API do?

without needing direct assistance from its creators.

Good documentation improves discoverability.

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
Documentation should match reality.

Incorrect documentation can be worse than missing documentation because it creates false expectations.

Documentation should evolve alongside the API.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Examples help consumers understand APIs more quickly.

Showing:

{
  "name": "Jonas"
}

is often more useful than describing the format in words.

Examples reduce ambiguity.

docs.title: Documentation as a Product
docs.text:
Documentation is not merely supporting material.

It is part of the API experience.

A professional API should be understandable without requiring consumers to inspect source code.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Two APIs provide identical functionality.

API A provides:

No documentation

API B provides:

  • Endpoint descriptions
  • Request examples
  • Response examples
  • Authentication instructions
  • Error descriptions

A new developer must integrate with one of these APIs.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why documentation matters.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Explain the purpose of API documentation
  • Identify problems caused by undocumented APIs
  • Describe how documentation improves developer experience

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Consider which API would require fewer questions.

Stronger Hint

Think about how quickly a new developer could become productive.

Almost There

Documentation reduces uncertainty and speeds up integration.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

API B is easier to consume because it communicates how the API works.

The developer can:

  • Discover available functionality
  • Understand request requirements
  • Anticipate responses
  • Learn without depending on other people

Documentation improves communication between API producers and API consumers.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Many documentation discussions start with tools and formats.

This exercise focuses on the underlying problem documentation solves: communication.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing a Create User endpoint.

The endpoint expects:

{
  "name": "Jonas",
  "email": "jonas@example.com"
}

and returns:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Jonas",
  "email": "jonas@example.com"
}

No documentation currently exists.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify what information should be documented.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • Describe endpoint behavior
  • Document expected inputs
  • Document expected outputs
  • Identify important consumer information

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Imagine someone has never seen the endpoint before.

Stronger Hint

What would a developer need before sending a request?

Almost There

Think about requests, responses, and expectations.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Useful documentation could include:

  • Endpoint purpose
  • Request format
  • Required fields
  • Example request
  • Example response
  • Possible error responses

Documentation should help consumers use the endpoint successfully.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Error handling is the capability of communicating failures in a predictable, useful, and consistent way.

Every API will encounter situations where it cannot successfully complete a request:

  • A resource does not exist
  • Input is invalid
  • Authentication fails
  • Authorization is denied
  • A dependency is unavailable
  • An unexpected system error occurs

Error handling exists to help API consumers understand what went wrong and what they should do next.

As APIs grow larger and serve more consumers, error handling becomes increasingly important because developers often spend more time diagnosing failures than reading successful responses.

Good error handling improves:

  • Developer experience
  • Reliability
  • Maintainability
  • API usability
  • System observability

Professional APIs treat errors as first-class API responses rather than afterthoughts.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine an API that returns user information.

A client requests:

GET /users/42

but user 42 does not exist.

Which response is better?

Option A:

{}

Option B:

{
  "message": "Error"
}

Option C:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "USER_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "User 42 does not exist"
  }
}

Option C provides useful information.

The client immediately understands:

  • What happened
  • Why it happened
  • What failed

Without clear error handling, API consumers are forced to guess what went wrong.

As systems become larger, inconsistent or vague errors make APIs significantly harder to use and maintain.

Error handling exists because failures are inevitable and clients need useful feedback.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
Errors allow systems to fail predictably instead of behaving unpredictably.

Clients should always know when an operation has failed.

docs.title: Maintainability
docs.text:
Consistent error structures make APIs easier to evolve and support over time.

Developers learn one pattern and can apply it everywhere.

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text:
Consumers should not need to learn a different error format for every endpoint.

A predictable API is easier to understand.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Good error handling communicates failures without exposing sensitive internal details.

For example:

✅ "Authentication failed"

instead of:

❌ "JWT signature validation failed in auth_service.py"

docs.title: User Experience
docs.text:
Human developers consume APIs.

Clear and actionable errors reduce frustration and improve productivity.

docs.title: Errors Are Normal
docs.text:
Failures are not exceptional in real systems.

Missing resources, invalid input, expired tokens, and service outages occur regularly.

Good APIs are designed with failure in mind.

docs.title: Client Errors
docs.text:
Client errors occur when the request cannot be processed because of something the client did.

Examples:

  • Invalid input
  • Missing required fields
  • Invalid credentials
  • Access denied
  • Resource not found

The client can potentially fix these issues.

docs.title: Server Errors
docs.text:
Server errors occur when something unexpected happens within the system.

Examples:

  • Database failures
  • Service outages
  • Unexpected exceptions
  • Infrastructure issues

Clients usually cannot resolve these problems themselves.

docs.title: Error Consistency
docs.text:
A consistent error structure makes APIs easier to consume.

For example:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "USER_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "User 42 does not exist"
  }
}

and

{
  "error": {
    "code": "INVALID_EMAIL",
    "message": "Email format is invalid"
  }
}

Both follow the same structure.

Consistency reduces cognitive load for API consumers.

docs.title: Actionable Errors
docs.text:
A good error helps the consumer understand what to do next.

Good:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "INVALID_EMAIL",
    "message": "Email must contain @"
  }
}

Less useful:

{
  "message": "Request failed"
}

Useful errors guide consumers toward successful requests.

docs.title: Error Design
docs.text:
When designing error responses, consider:

  • Is the error clear?
  • Is the error consistent?
  • Is the error actionable?
  • Is the error safe to expose?
  • Would another developer understand it quickly?

Error handling is ultimately a communication problem.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A client requests:

GET /products/9999

but product 9999 does not exist.

The API team is debating how the API should respond.

Possible responses include:

{}

{
  "message": "Error"
}

{
  "error": {
    "code": "PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Product 9999 does not exist"
  }
}

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why clear error responses are important.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:

  • Explain why error handling exists
  • Identify weaknesses in vague error responses
  • Recognize characteristics of useful error responses

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Stronger Hint

Which response helps you understand exactly what failed?

Almost There

The best response clearly explains the problem without requiring guesswork.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The third response is the most useful.

It clearly communicates:

  • What failed
  • Why it failed
  • Which resource caused the problem

Clear communication is one of the primary goals of error handling.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Many developers initially think about successful API responses.

Professional API engineers must also think about failure scenarios.

Understanding this mindset shift is the foundation of effective error handling.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Filtering allows API consumers to request only the data they care about.

Without filtering, APIs often return large collections of data, forcing consumers to retrieve information they do not need and discard it themselves.

Filtering exists because most API consumers are not asking:

"Give me everything."

They are asking:

"Give me the specific information that matches my needs."

API engineers should care about filtering because it improves usability, reduces unnecessary data transfer, and helps consumers find relevant information efficiently.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine an online bookstore API.

GET /books

The API contains:

  • 250,000 books
  • multiple genres
  • multiple authors
  • books from many years

A consumer wants:

  • science fiction books
  • books published after 2020
  • books by a specific author

Without filtering:

Retrieve all books
        ↓
Process results locally
        ↓
Discard most of the data

This wastes:

  • bandwidth
  • processing time
  • API resources
  • developer effort

As APIs grow, returning everything becomes increasingly impractical.

Filtering solves this problem by allowing consumers to request relevant subsets of data.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Filtering improves:

✅ User Experience

Consumers can quickly find relevant information.

✅ Performance

Less data is transferred over the network.

✅ Scalability

Large datasets become more manageable.

✅ Maintainability

Clear filtering rules create predictable behavior.

✅ API Adoption

APIs are easier and more enjoyable to use when consumers can efficiently locate the data they need.

docs.title: Filterable Fields
docs.text:
Not every field should be filterable.

Examples:

author
category
status
created_date
price

A good API intentionally chooses which fields can be filtered.

docs.title: Exact Match Filtering
docs.text:
Used when values must match exactly.

Example:

status = active

Useful for:

  • states
  • categories
  • identifiers

docs.title: Range Filtering
docs.text:
Used when values exist within a range.

Examples:

price >= 100

created_after = 2024-01-01

Useful for:

  • dates
  • numbers
  • measurements

docs.title: Multi-Filter Queries
docs.text:
Consumers often need more than one filter.

Example:

Active users
created after January 1st
from Denmark

Combining filters can significantly improve data discovery.

docs.title: Optional Filtering
docs.text:
Most filters should be optional.

Example:

No filters
    ↓
Return all available items

Some filters
    ↓
Return matching items

This creates flexible APIs.

docs.title: Invalid Filters
docs.text:
API engineers must decide:

Ignore invalid filters?

Or

Return an error?

Consistency is usually more important than the specific decision.

Consumers should understand how the API behaves.

docs.title: Filtering vs Search
docs.text:
Filtering and search often look similar but solve different problems.

Filtering:

Find records matching known criteria

Examples:

status=active

category=books

Search:

Find records containing unknown information

Examples:

search=python

search=fastapi

Understanding this distinction helps produce better API designs.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a task management API.

The endpoint:

GET /tasks

returns every task in the system.

Users complain that finding open tasks assigned to them requires downloading hundreds of tasks and manually filtering the results.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why filtering exists.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • explain why returning all data is problematic
  • describe how filtering improves API usability
  • identify situations where filtering would be valuable

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Do users usually want every record?

Stronger Hint

Think about what happens as the number of tasks grows.

Almost There

Filtering allows consumers to request only relevant data.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Returning all tasks becomes increasingly inefficient as datasets grow.

Filtering allows users to retrieve only:

  • open tasks
  • their own tasks
  • tasks with a specific priority

This improves usability, performance, and efficiency.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Many API capabilities exist because growth creates problems.

Filtering is one of the first capabilities that becomes necessary when datasets become larger than a consumer can comfortably process.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:

Consumers want to retrieve products by:

  • category
  • price range

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Design a filtering strategy.

docs.title: Success Criteria

docs.title: Hints

Stronger Hint

Some fields are categories while others represent numerical ranges.

Almost There

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

A reasonable design might allow:

  • category filtering
  • availability filtering
  • minimum price filtering
  • maximum price filtering

This provides flexibility without exposing every field for filtering.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
API engineers must intentionally choose which filtering capabilities provide value.

Effective filtering is a design decision, not simply a technical feature.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building an employee directory API.

Consumers want to:

  • filter by department
  • filter by office location
  • filter by employment status
  • sort results
  • paginate large result sets

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Design a complete data discovery experience.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • design a consistent request experience
  • reason about tradeoffs

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Filtering rarely exists by itself.

Stronger Hint

Almost There

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

A complete solution combines:

  • filtering to narrow results
  • sorting to organize results
  • pagination to limit response size

These capabilities work together to help users discover data efficiently.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Real-world APIs rarely use capabilities in isolation.

Professional API design often involves combining multiple capabilities into a coherent experience.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your organization operates dozens of APIs.

Many teams have implemented filtering differently:

  • inconsistent error behavior

Consumers find the APIs difficult to learn.

Do all APIs behave the same way?

Stronger Hint

Consumers benefit when patterns are predictable.

Consistent filtering conventions reduce learning effort across APIs.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The organization should establish common standards for:

  • parameter naming
  • date formats
  • range filters
  • error responses
  • filtering behavior

Consistency improves maintainability and consumer experience across the API ecosystem.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
As organizations scale, consistency becomes increasingly important.

Reusable filtering patterns help teams create predictable APIs and reduce friction for API consumers.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Filtering solves the problem of data overload.

Without filtering, consumers often receive more information than they need.

Filtering helps API engineers create APIs that are:

  • easier to use
  • more efficient
  • more scalable
  • more maintainable

A professional API does not simply expose data.

It provides consumers with practical ways to discover the data they actually need.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Pagination is a capability that allows APIs to return large collections of data in smaller, manageable chunks.

Without pagination, APIs may attempt to return thousands, hundreds of thousands, or even millions of records in a single response.

Pagination exists because datasets grow.

What works for 10 records often becomes unusable for 10,000 records.

API engineers should care about pagination because it improves performance, scalability, user experience, and system reliability.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine an e-commerce platform with:

5 million products

A consumer makes the request:

GET /products

Without pagination, the API attempts to return all products at once.

This creates problems:

  • slow responses
  • large network transfers
  • excessive memory usage
  • poor user experience
  • increased infrastructure costs

Even if the request succeeds, the consumer probably cannot meaningfully use all of the data at once.

They typically want:

Show me the first 20 products.

Then the next 20.

Then the next 20.

Pagination solves this problem by allowing datasets to be consumed incrementally.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Pagination improves:

✅ Performance

Smaller responses are generally faster to process and transfer.

✅ Scalability

APIs can handle larger datasets without overwhelming infrastructure.

✅ Reliability

Large responses are less likely to cause timeouts or resource exhaustion.

✅ User Experience

Consumers can navigate data in manageable pieces.

✅ Consistency

APIs provide predictable ways to browse large collections.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
Pagination divides a large collection into smaller subsets.

Example:

Page 1
Items 1-20

Page 2
Items 21-40

Page 3
Items 41-60

Consumers can retrieve data incrementally.

docs.title: Page Size
docs.text:
Page size determines how many items appear in a single response.

Examples:

10 items

20 items

50 items

100 items

Smaller pages reduce response size.

Larger pages reduce the number of requests.

Choosing an appropriate page size is a design tradeoff.

docs.title: Offset Pagination
docs.text:
Offset pagination allows consumers to skip a number of records.

Conceptually:

Start at record 100

Return the next 20 records

Benefits:

  • easy to understand
  • easy to implement

Challenges:

  • can become expensive on very large datasets
  • can produce inconsistent results when data changes frequently

docs.title: Cursor Pagination
docs.text:
Cursor pagination uses a reference point instead of a record count.

Conceptually:

Return items after this specific record

Benefits:

  • performs well on larger datasets
  • works well with frequently changing data

Challenges:

  • more complex to design
  • less intuitive for consumers

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Consumers often need information about the result set.

Examples:

Current page

Page size

Total items

Next page available?

Pagination is usually more useful when accompanied by helpful metadata.

docs.title: Sorting and Pagination
docs.text:
Pagination often depends on a predictable ordering.

Example:

Newest first

Oldest first

Alphabetical

Without a consistent order:

Page 1 today

Page 1 tomorrow

might contain different records.

Pagination and sorting frequently work together.

docs.title: Pagination and Filtering
docs.text:
Pagination rarely exists in isolation.

Consumers often:

Filter results
        ↓
Sort results
        ↓
Paginate results

Understanding how these capabilities interact is important when designing APIs.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A reporting API currently returns every invoice in the system.

The company now has more than 500,000 invoices.

Consumers complain that requests are becoming slow and sometimes fail.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why pagination exists.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • explain the problem caused by large result sets
  • describe how pagination improves scalability
  • recognize situations where pagination becomes necessary

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think about what happens as the amount of data grows.

Stronger Hint

Do users usually need every record at the same time?

Almost There

Pagination allows consumers to retrieve manageable portions of a dataset.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Returning every invoice causes increasingly large responses as the dataset grows.

Pagination reduces response sizes by dividing the dataset into smaller portions that can be retrieved incrementally.

This improves performance, reliability, and usability.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Many API capabilities emerge as systems grow.

Pagination is one of the most common solutions to problems caused by large datasets.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:

250,000 customers

docs.title: Objective

docs.title: Hints

Stronger Hint

Almost There

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

A reasonable pagination strategy might:

  • divide results into pages
  • allow consumers to select page size
  • return metadata about the result set

This creates a more scalable and user-friendly API.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Pagination is not just a technical feature.

It is an API design decision that directly affects usability and performance.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing a product catalog API.

Consumers want to:

  • search products
  • filter products by category
  • sort products by price
  • browse large result sets

docs.title: Objective

  • combine pagination with filtering
  • combine pagination with sorting
  • reason about API usability

docs.title: Hints

Stronger Hint

Think about the order in which filtering, sorting, and pagination occur.

Almost There

Consumers first narrow data, then order it, then browse it.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

A complete solution might:

  • filter products
  • sort the filtered results
  • paginate the sorted dataset

These capabilities work together to make large datasets manageable and useful.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Real-world APIs rarely implement pagination by itself.

Pagination is most valuable when combined with other data-discovery capabilities.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
An organization operates dozens of APIs.

Each team implemented pagination differently:

  • different parameter names
  • different page sizes
  • different metadata structures
  • different navigation patterns

API consumers struggle to switch between services.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify reusable pagination patterns.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • identify consistency problems
  • define shared pagination standards
  • explain why reusable conventions matter

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Do all APIs behave the same way?

Stronger Hint

Consumers benefit from predictable interfaces.

Almost There

Consistent pagination patterns reduce learning effort across APIs.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The organization should establish common conventions for:

  • page size limits
  • metadata fields
  • parameter naming
  • result ordering
  • navigation behavior

This creates a more predictable API ecosystem and improves maintainability.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
As organizations scale, consistency becomes increasingly valuable.

Reusable pagination patterns help both API consumers and API engineers.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Pagination solves the problem of large datasets.

Without pagination, APIs may become:

  • slow
  • expensive
  • difficult to use
  • difficult to scale

Pagination allows data to be consumed incrementally and predictably.

Professional API engineers must understand:

  • when pagination is necessary
  • common pagination strategies
  • pagination tradeoffs
  • how pagination interacts with filtering and sorting

A well-designed API does not simply expose data.

It makes large datasets practical to explore.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Routing is one of the foundational capabilities of API Engineering.

Every API receives requests from clients.

Examples:

  • Web applications
  • Mobile applications
  • Other APIs
  • Internal services
  • Automated systems

When a request arrives, the API must decide:

What functionality should handle this request?

Routing is the capability that answers this question.

Without routing, an API has no way of directing incoming requests to the correct functionality.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine an online bookstore API.

Clients need to:

  • View all books
  • View a specific book
  • Create a book
  • Update a book
  • Delete a book

A request arrives:

GET /books/123

How does the API know that:

Book #123 should be retrieved

rather than:

Create a new book

or:

List all books

Routing provides the structure that allows APIs to direct requests to the correct operation.

Without routing:

  • Requests become ambiguous
  • APIs become difficult to maintain
  • Consumers become confused
  • Functionality becomes hard to discover

docs.title: Why Routing Matters
docs.text:
Routing helps ensure:

✅ Requests reach the correct functionality

✅ APIs remain organized as they grow

✅ Consumers can discover resources easily

✅ Functionality remains predictable

✅ URLs communicate intent clearly

Well-designed routing is one of the foundations of a usable API.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
An endpoint is a specific location within an API.

Examples:

GET /books

GET /books/123

POST /books

Each endpoint represents a specific capability exposed by the API.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Most APIs expose resources.

Examples:

Users

Books

Orders

Products

Invoices

Routes are often designed around resources rather than actions.

Instead of:

GET /getBooks

many APIs prefer:

GET /books

because the route represents a resource.

docs.title: HTTP Methods
docs.text:
The same route can perform different actions depending on the HTTP method.

Examples:

GET /books

Retrieve books.

POST /books

Create a book.

PUT /books/123

Update book 123.

DELETE /books/123

Delete book 123.

docs.title: Path Parameters
docs.text:
Some routes operate on specific resources.

Example:

GET /users/42

The value:

42

is a path parameter.

Path parameters identify a specific resource.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Query parameters modify how a route behaves.

Example:

GET /books?category=python

The route remains:

/books

but the query parameter changes what data is returned.

Common uses:

  • Filtering
  • Searching
  • Sorting
  • Pagination

docs.title: Route Design
docs.text:
Good routes are:

✅ Predictable

✅ Consistent

✅ Easy to understand

Examples:

GET /users

GET /users/42

POST /users

DELETE /users/42

Poor routes often become difficult to learn and maintain.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You join a team that maintains a books API.

You discover the following routes:

GET /books

GET /books/123

POST /books

DELETE /books/123

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand what each route is responsible for.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • identify the resource
  • explain the purpose of each route
  • identify which routes operate on a specific resource

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Focus on the URL path first.

Stronger Hint

Notice that all routes relate to the same resource.

Almost There

Some routes operate on the collection while others operate on a specific item.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Resource:

Books

Routes:

GET /books

Retrieves all books.

GET /books/123

Retrieves a specific book.

POST /books

Creates a new book.

DELETE /books/123

Deletes a specific book.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Routing is one of the first capabilities every API engineer must understand.

It answers a fundamental question:

How do requests reach the correct functionality?

Strong routing helps make APIs:

  • Predictable
  • Consistent
  • Discoverable
  • Maintainable

Almost every other API capability depends on routing.

For example:

Routing
    ↓
Validation

    ↓

    ↓
Authorization

Learning routing is therefore not about learning framework syntax.

It is about understanding one of the foundational capabilities of API Engineering.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Testing is a capability that allows API engineers to verify that an API behaves as expected.

As APIs grow, changes are constantly introduced:

  • new endpoints
  • new validations
  • new authentication rules
  • new business logic

Testing exists because every change introduces risk.

Without testing, API engineers must rely on manual verification and assumptions.

API engineers should care about testing because it provides confidence that APIs continue working correctly as systems evolve.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine a task management API.

A developer adds a new validation rule:

Task titles must contain at least 3 characters.

The change appears harmless.

The application deploys successfully.

Hours later, users report that creating tasks no longer works.

The application starts returning unexpected errors.

The developer accidentally broke existing functionality.

Nothing in the deployment process detected the issue before release.

Testing exists because APIs change frequently, and every change introduces the possibility of unintended consequences.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Testing improves:

✅ Reliability

Changes can be verified before deployment.

✅ Maintainability

Developers can refactor with greater confidence.

✅ Consistency

Expected behavior becomes documented and repeatable.

✅ Quality

Bugs are discovered earlier.

✅ Developer Confidence

Teams spend less time wondering whether changes broke existing functionality.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Testing is fundamentally about verification.

A test answers a question such as:

Does this behavior work as expected?

Example:

Can users create tasks?

Can invalid data be rejected?

Can unauthorized requests be blocked?

docs.title: Expected Behavior
docs.text:
A test defines what should happen.

Example:

Given valid input

Expect success

or

Given invalid input

Expect a validation error

This creates a clear definition of correct behavior.

docs.title: Automated Testing
docs.text:
Tests can be executed repeatedly.

Instead of manually checking behavior after every change:

Developer changes code
        ↓
Tests run
        ↓
Problems are detected

This greatly reduces risk.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
A regression occurs when previously working functionality stops working.

Example:

Feature works today

Code changes tomorrow

Feature now fails

Testing helps detect regressions before users encounter them.

docs.title: Test Coverage
docs.text:
Coverage describes how much of a system is exercised by tests.

Examples:

Routes

Validation

Authentication

Authorization

Business logic

High coverage does not guarantee quality.

However, important behavior should generally be tested.

docs.title: Happy Paths
docs.text:
A happy path tests expected and successful behavior.

Example:

Valid request

Expected success response

These tests verify that the API works when used correctly.

docs.title: Edge Cases
docs.text:
Real-world systems encounter unusual situations.

Examples:

Missing fields

Invalid values

Unauthenticated requests

Unexpected input

Testing edge cases often reveals issues before users find them.

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text:
Perhaps the most important outcome of testing is confidence.

Testing does not prove that software is perfect.

Instead it provides evidence that important behavior continues to function as expected.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
An API team frequently makes changes to an application.

Before every release they manually test several endpoints.

Sometimes they forget to test important scenarios.

Production issues occur regularly.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why testing exists.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • explain the risks of manual verification alone
  • describe how testing reduces change risk
  • identify situations where testing provides value

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

What happens when developers forget to manually check something?

Stronger Hint

Systems often become more complex over time.

Almost There

Testing provides a repeatable way to verify behavior.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Manual verification depends on people remembering every scenario.

Testing provides repeatable validation that can be executed whenever changes occur.

This reduces the likelihood of bugs reaching production.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Many teams only appreciate testing after experiencing costly regressions.

Understanding why testing exists is more important than learning testing tools.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing an API that allows users to create products.

The API requires:

  • a product name
  • a positive price

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify what should be tested.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • identify successful scenarios
  • identify failure scenarios
  • reason about expected behavior

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think about both valid and invalid requests.

Stronger Hint

What happens if the price is negative?

Almost There

Tests should verify both success and failure behavior.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Useful tests might include:

  • valid product creation
  • missing product name
  • negative price
  • invalid data types

These tests verify both expected behavior and error handling.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Professional testing involves thinking carefully about expected and unexpected inputs.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing an API with:

  • authentication
  • authorization
  • validation
  • filtering
  • pagination

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Develop a testing strategy.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • identify important areas to test
  • combine multiple API capabilities
  • reason about risk and confidence

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

APIs are usually more than individual endpoints.

Stronger Hint

Consider what happens when capabilities interact.

Almost There

Important system behaviors often involve multiple capabilities working together.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

A complete testing strategy might verify:

  • authenticated access
  • authorization rules
  • validation behavior
  • filtering behavior
  • pagination behavior
  • expected error responses

This provides confidence that the API behaves correctly across multiple capabilities.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Real-world APIs depend on many capabilities working together.

Testing should reflect how the system is actually used.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
An organization operates dozens of APIs.

Every team tests differently.

Some teams:

  • test manually
  • test inconsistently
  • skip testing under deadlines

Software quality varies significantly.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify reusable testing practices.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • identify testing consistency problems
  • recognize reusable testing patterns
  • explain the value of standardization

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

What happens when every team invents its own process?

Stronger Hint

Consistent testing practices reduce risk.

Almost There

Organizations benefit when testing becomes repeatable and predictable.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The organization should establish shared practices for:

  • automated testing
  • critical API behaviors
  • failure scenarios
  • test execution during development
  • release validation

Consistent testing improves reliability across the entire API ecosystem.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Testing scales best when it becomes a repeatable organizational capability rather than an individual developer habit.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Testing solves the problem of uncertainty.

Without testing, API changes introduce risk that may not be discovered until users encounter failures.

Testing helps API engineers:

  • verify behavior
  • prevent regressions
  • improve reliability
  • increase confidence
  • evolve systems safely

Professional APIs are rarely built once and left unchanged.

They are continuously improved and modified.

Testing provides the safety net that allows those improvements to happen responsibly.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validation is one of the most important capabilities in API Engineering.

Every API accepts data from external clients:

  • Users
  • Frontend applications
  • Mobile apps
  • Other APIs
  • Automated systems

Without validation, invalid or unexpected data can enter the system and cause errors, security issues, and unreliable behavior.

The goal of validation is to ensure that incoming and outgoing data matches the expectations of the API.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine a user registration API.

A client sends:

{
  "email": "not-an-email",
  "age": -5
}

Should this data be accepted?

Most likely not.

Without validation:

  • Bad data enters the database
  • Bugs become harder to diagnose
  • Unexpected behavior occurs
  • Security risks may increase

Validation helps detect problems as early as possible.

docs.title: Why Validation Matters
docs.text:
Validation helps ensure that:

✅ Required fields are present

✅ Data has the correct type

✅ Values are within acceptable ranges

✅ Business rules are enforced

✅ Consumers receive useful error messages

A well-designed API makes invalid states difficult to create.

docs.title: Common Validation Rules
docs.text: Many APIs use validation rules such as:

docs.title: Required Fields
docs.text:
A field must be provided.

Example:

{
  "username": ""
}

The API may require:

username is required

docs.title: Data Types
docs.text:
A value must be a specific type.

Examples:

name → string

age → integer

active → boolean

docs.title: Length Constraints
docs.text:
A value must be a certain length.

Examples:

Password must be at least 12 characters.

Username must be between 3 and 50 characters.

docs.title: Range Constraints
docs.text:
A value must be within an acceptable range.

Examples:

Age must be greater than 0.

Percentage must be between 0 and 100.

docs.title: Format Validation
docs.text:
A value must follow a specific format.

Examples:

Email addresses

Phone numbers

URLs

Dates

docs.title: Request Validation
docs.text:
Request validation occurs when data enters the API.

Example:

POST /users

Request body:

{
  "name": "Jonas",
  "email": "jonas@example.com"
}

The API verifies that:

  • Required fields exist
  • Types are correct
  • Formats are valid
  • Business rules are satisfied

Only then is processing allowed to continue.

Request validation is often the most visible form of validation within APIs.

docs.title: Response Validation
docs.text:
Validation can also occur when data leaves the API.

Example:

{
  "id": 123,
  "email": "jonas@example.com"
}

The API may validate the response before sending it to clients.

Benefits include:

  • Consistent responses
  • Fewer contract violations
  • More reliable API consumers

Response validation is especially useful for large systems where multiple components generate data.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your company has a user registration API.

Users occasionally submit invalid data:

{
  "email": "not-an-email",
  "age": -5
}

The API currently accepts the request.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify which fields should be validated.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
You should be able to:

  • identify invalid fields
  • explain why they are invalid
  • suggest appropriate validation rules

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think about which values might cause problems if stored in a database.

Stronger Hint

Consider email formats and numeric ranges.

Almost There

A valid email should look like an email address. Age typically should not be negative.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Validation rules could include:

  • Email must follow a valid email format
  • Age must be greater than or equal to 0

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Validation begins by recognizing bad data before thinking about implementation.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing an API for registering new users.

Each user contains:

  • username
  • email
  • age

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Create a validation plan.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Define:

  • required fields
  • length rules
  • format rules
  • range rules
Small Hint

Stronger Hint

Consider username length and email format requirements.

Almost There

Think about realistic limits such as:

  • username length
  • minimum age
  • email format

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Example rules:

  • username required
  • username 3-50 characters
  • email required
  • email must be valid
  • age must be >= 0

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: API engineers often design validation before writing code.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing a blog platform API.

A blog post contains:

  • title
  • content
  • author
  • tags

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Design a complete validation strategy.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:

  • required fields

  • business rules
  • response validation needs

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think about which fields should never be empty.

Stronger Hint

Consider title length and minimum content length.

Almost There

Blog posts with empty titles or content probably should not be accepted.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Example:

  • title required
  • title max 200 characters
  • content required
  • content min 50 characters
  • tags optional
  • maximum 10 tags

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Real APIs typically validate multiple related fields simultaneously.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your organization has:

  • User APIs
  • Product APIs
  • Billing APIs

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify validation patterns that could be standardized.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:

Stronger Hint

Almost There

docs.title: Solution

Solution

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Strong API ecosystems rely on consistent validation patterns.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Validation is often one of the first lines of defense in an API.

Strong validation helps create APIs that are:

  • Predictable
  • Reliable
  • Easier to use
  • Easier to maintain

Regardless of framework, every API engineer eventually faces the same challenge:

How do I ensure that incoming and outgoing
data is valid?

Learning validation is therefore not about learning a framework feature.

It is about learning a fundamental API Engineering capability.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Versioning is a capability that allows APIs to evolve without unexpectedly breaking existing consumers.

As APIs mature, requirements change:

  • fields are added
  • fields are removed
  • endpoints change
  • business rules evolve

Versioning exists because APIs are long-lived systems.

An API may have consumers that depend on its behavior for months or years.

API engineers should care about versioning because it helps balance innovation with stability.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Imagine a customer management API.

An endpoint currently returns:

{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "Jane Doe"
}

Many applications consume this API.

Months later, the team decides to replace:

"name"

with:

"first_name",
"last_name"

The change seems reasonable.

However:

Existing applications fail
        ↓
Unexpected errors occur
        ↓
Customers become frustrated

The API team improved the API.

But they also broke existing consumers.

Versioning exists because APIs often need to evolve while continuing to support systems that depend on previous behavior.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Versioning improves:

✅ Reliability

Consumers can continue using known behavior.

✅ Stability

Changes can be introduced more safely.

✅ Maintainability

API evolution becomes more structured.

✅ Consumer Trust

Consumers are less likely to experience unexpected breaking changes.

✅ Long-Term Sustainability

APIs can adapt to new requirements without constantly disrupting users.

docs.title: API Evolution
docs.text:
APIs rarely remain unchanged.

Over time teams may:

  • add features
  • improve designs
  • fix mistakes
  • support new requirements

Versioning provides a strategy for managing these changes.

docs.title: Breaking Changes
docs.text:
A breaking change is a change that causes existing consumers to stop working correctly.

Examples:

Removing a field

Renaming a field

Removing an endpoint

Changing request formats

Changing response formats

Breaking changes are one of the primary reasons versioning exists.

docs.title: Non-Breaking Changes
docs.text:
Some changes can be introduced without affecting consumers.

Examples:

Adding a new optional field

Adding a new endpoint

Adding new filtering options

These changes often do not require a new API version.

API engineers should understand the difference.

docs.title: Backward Compatibility
docs.text:
Backward compatibility means existing consumers continue to work after changes are introduced.

Example:

Version 1 clients continue functioning

While

Version 2 introduces improvements

Maintaining backward compatibility can reduce disruption for consumers.

docs.title: Multiple Versions
docs.text:
Organizations frequently support more than one version at a time.

Conceptually:

Version 1
    ↓
Legacy consumers

Version 2
    ↓
New consumers

This allows migration to occur gradually rather than all at once.

docs.title: Deprecation
docs.text:
Older versions rarely live forever.

API teams often:

Announce deprecation
        ↓
Provide migration guidance
        ↓
Retire older versions

Versioning is not only about creating versions.

It is also about managing their lifecycle.

docs.title: Versioning Strategies
docs.text:
There are multiple ways to expose API versions.

Common approaches include:

Version in URL

Version in headers

Version in content negotiation

Each strategy has advantages and tradeoffs.

The specific implementation is less important than maintaining a clear and consistent approach.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
Versioning is partly a technical problem.

It is also a communication problem.

Consumers need to know:

  • what changed
  • why it changed
  • when older versions will be retired
  • how to migrate

Good communication is often as important as the versioning mechanism itself.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your organization provides an API used by dozens of customer applications.

The API team wants to rename several response fields to improve clarity.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why versioning exists.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • explain why breaking changes are risky
  • describe how versioning protects consumers
  • recognize when API evolution creates compatibility concerns

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

What happens if an application expects data that no longer exists?

Stronger Hint

Not all consumers can update immediately.

Almost There

Versioning allows APIs to evolve while minimizing disruptions.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Renaming response fields may break existing applications.

Versioning allows newer behavior to be introduced without immediately removing older behavior.

This provides consumers with time to adapt and migrate.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
APIs often serve many consumers with different update schedules.

Versioning exists largely to manage change responsibly.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing a public API expected to be used by external partners.

The API will likely evolve over time.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Determine when versioning should be considered.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • identify changes that may impact consumers
  • distinguish between breaking and non-breaking changes
  • explain why versioning may be necessary

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Consider changes to request and response formats.

Stronger Hint

Not every change requires a new version.

Almost There

Versioning becomes most important when changes could cause existing integrations to fail.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Versioning should be considered whenever changes may break existing consumers.

Examples include:

  • removing fields
  • changing field names
  • altering request structures
  • removing endpoints

Non-breaking additions may not require a new version.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: API engineers must understand which changes affect compatibility and which changes can safely be introduced within an existing version.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are designing an API platform with:

  • authentication
  • filtering
  • pagination
  • reporting endpoints

The platform serves both internal teams and external customers.

New requirements are expected every year.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Design an API evolution strategy.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • reason about long-term API evolution
  • identify compatibility risks
  • balance innovation with stability

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Consider how consumers will handle future changes.

Stronger Hint

Different consumers may upgrade at different times.
