docs.title: FastAPI Authentication
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Authentication capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • The problem authentication solves
  • Why authentication matters
  • General API engineering concepts behind authentication

Authentication is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
FastAPI provides built-in tools that make it easier to implement authentication in a consistent and maintainable way.

Authentication can quickly become complex when developers must manually handle:

  • Credentials
  • Identity verification
  • Protected endpoints
  • Security workflows

FastAPI provides reusable building blocks that reduce boilerplate and encourage clean authentication patterns.

Benefits include:

✅ Built-in security utilities

✅ Reusable authentication dependencies

✅ OpenAPI integration

✅ Automatic documentation support

✅ Cleaner endpoint code

✅ Better maintainability

✅ Consistent authentication workflows

FastAPI encourages developers to separate authentication logic from business logic.

docs.title: Depends
docs.text:
Depends() is one of the most important concepts in FastAPI authentication.

Authentication checks are often implemented as reusable dependencies.

Example:

from fastapi import Depends

@app.get("/profile")
def get_profile(user=Depends(get_current_user)):
    return user

This allows authentication logic to be reused across many endpoints.

docs.title: OAuth2PasswordBearer
docs.text:
OAuth2PasswordBearer extracts authentication tokens from incoming requests.

Example:

from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(
    tokenUrl="token"
)

FastAPI automatically looks for a bearer token in the request.

docs.title: Access Tokens
docs.text:
Authentication systems commonly issue tokens after successful authentication.

Example:

Authorization: Bearer abc123

The token becomes evidence of the caller's identity.

docs.title: Current User Dependencies
docs.text:
Many APIs create reusable functions that retrieve the authenticated user.

Example:

def get_current_user(
    token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)
):
    ...

This allows endpoints to work with authenticated identities rather than raw tokens.

docs.title: Security Utilities
docs.text:
FastAPI provides additional security helpers through:

fastapi.security

These utilities simplify authentication implementation and integrate with OpenAPI documentation.

docs.title: Protected Endpoints
docs.text:
Protected endpoints require successful authentication before processing requests.

Example:

@app.get("/me")
def get_me(
    user=Depends(get_current_user)
):
    return user

Only authenticated callers can access the endpoint.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You encounter the following code:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

app = FastAPI()

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(
    tokenUrl="token"
)


@app.get("/profile")
def get_profile(
    token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)
):
    return {
        "token": token
    }

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand how FastAPI extracts authentication information from requests.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:

  • What OAuth2PasswordBearer does

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Stronger Hint

Almost There

The token is being extracted before the endpoint executes.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

OAuth2PasswordBearer extracts a bearer token from the incoming request.

Depends() injects the resulting value into the endpoint.

This allows endpoints to receive authentication information without manually parsing request headers.

docs.text:

Different teams implement authentication differently.

Some endpoints parse tokens manually.

docs.text:
Solution

One possible approach is to standardize:

oauth2_scheme

and:

get_current_user()

across all services.

Example:

def get_current_user(
    token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)
):
    ...

Endpoints can then use:

user = Depends(get_current_user)

This creates a consistent authentication approach across many APIs.

docs.text:
Professional APIs typically rely on reusable security patterns rather than isolated implementations.

Consistency improves maintainability and reduces errors.

docs.text:

Example:

@app.get("/tasks")
def get_tasks():

    # authentication logic

    # business logic

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Move authentication into reusable dependencies.

user = Depends(get_current_user)

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:

def get_current_user():
    ...

Reuse them everywhere.

docs.text: The concepts are closely related.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Separate responsibilities.

Authentication:

Who are you?

Authorization:

What are you allowed to do?

Authenticate first.

Authorize second.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text: Create clear patterns and consistently apply them across protected endpoints.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: Developers focus only on retrieving tokens.

docs.title: Better Approach

Authentication is about establishing trust, not merely reading credentials.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
FastAPI provides powerful tools for implementing authentication through:

  • Depends
  • OAuth2PasswordBearer
  • Security utilities
  • Reusable dependencies

These tools allow developers to separate authentication logic from business logic and create reusable security patterns.

As APIs grow, authentication becomes increasingly important because systems must reliably identify callers before granting access to protected functionality.

Understanding FastAPI's authentication tools helps you build APIs that are:

Authentication is one of the foundational capabilities of professional API engineering, and FastAPI provides a clean and structured way to implement it.

docs.title: FastAPI Authorization
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Authorization capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • The problem authorization solves
  • Why authorization matters
  • General API engineering concepts behind authorization

Authorization is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
FastAPI provides several tools that make authorization easier to implement and maintain.

Once a user has been authenticated, APIs often need to enforce rules such as:

  • Administrators can delete resources
  • Managers can view reports
  • Users can only access their own data

FastAPI's dependency system makes it easy to centralize authorization decisions and reuse them across many endpoints.

Benefits include:

✅ Reusable authorization logic

✅ Cleaner endpoint code

✅ Better maintainability

✅ Consistent access control

✅ Easier testing

✅ Reduced duplication

✅ Integration with authentication dependencies

Authorization rules can be implemented once and reused throughout the application.

docs.title: Depends
docs.text:
Most authorization logic is implemented using dependencies.

Example:

from fastapi import Depends

@app.get("/reports")
def get_reports(
    user=Depends(require_manager)
):
    ...

The dependency determines whether access should be granted.

docs.title: Current User
docs.text:
Authorization decisions usually depend on the authenticated user.

Example:

def get_current_user():
    ...

Authorization typically begins by identifying who is making the request.

docs.title: Role Checks
docs.text:
A common authorization strategy is role-based access control.

Example:

if user["role"] != "admin":
    ...

Roles often represent broad groups of permissions.

Examples:

User
Manager
Administrator

docs.title: Permission Checks
docs.text:
Some systems make decisions based on permissions rather than roles.

Example:

if "delete_user" not in user["permissions"]:
    ...

Permissions often represent specific actions.

docs.title: HTTPException
docs.text:
Unauthorized actions are commonly rejected using HTTPException.

Example:

raise HTTPException(
    status_code=403,
    detail="Access denied"
)

Authorization failures should communicate that access is not permitted.

docs.title: Ownership Checks
docs.text:
Many APIs allow users to access their own resources while restricting access to resources owned by others.

Example:

if task.owner_id != user.id:
    ...

Ownership is one of the most common authorization patterns.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You encounter the following code:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends

app = FastAPI()


def get_current_user():
    return {
        "username": "jonas",
        "role": "admin"
    }


@app.delete("/users/{user_id}")
def delete_user(
    user_id: int,
    user=Depends(get_current_user)
):
    return {
        "deleted": user_id
    }

A user is authenticated before reaching the endpoint.

No authorization checks exist.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand why authentication alone is not enough.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to explain:

  • What information is available about the current user
  • Why authorization is missing
  • What risks may exist

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

The API knows who the user is.

Stronger Hint

Consider whether every authenticated user should delete users.

Almost There

Authentication establishes identity, but access rules are still missing.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The endpoint knows who the caller is because get_current_user() provides identity information.

However, the endpoint never checks whether the user is allowed to delete users.

Authorization is required to enforce access control decisions.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
The goal is to understand the distinction between authentication and authorization.

FastAPI often uses dependencies for both, but they solve different problems.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:

@app.delete("/users/{user_id}")

    }

docs.text: Add authorization logic.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:

  • Check user roles
  • Deny access when appropriate
  • Return a useful error response

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:

Stronger Hint

Use an authorization check before continuing.

Almost There

docs.title: Solution
Why This Exercise Exists

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A Task API contains:

  • View task
  • Update task
  • Delete task

Users should only access their own tasks.

Administrators should access any task.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Combine ownership and role-based authorization.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to combine:

  • Current user dependencies
  • Role checks
  • Ownership checks

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Not all authorization requires roles.

Stronger Hint

Almost There

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution 
def can_access_task(
    task,
    user
):

    if user["role"] == "admin":
        return True

    return task.owner_id == user["id"]

The authorization logic now considers:

  • Administrative access
  • Resource ownership

This creates more realistic access control behavior.

FastAPI provides excellent support for authorization through:

As systems grow, authorization becomes increasingly important because different users often require different access levels.

docs.title: FastAPI Documentation
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Documentation capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • The problem documentation solves
  • Why documentation matters
  • General API engineering concepts behind documentation

Documentation is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
One of FastAPI's most powerful features is its built-in documentation support.

Unlike many frameworks where documentation is added later through external tools, FastAPI generates API documentation automatically from your code.

Benefits include:

✅ Less boilerplate

✅ Automatic OpenAPI generation

✅ Interactive API exploration

✅ Automatically documented request models

✅ Automatically documented response models

✅ Better API discoverability

✅ Improved maintainability

FastAPI encourages developers to treat documentation as part of API development rather than an afterthought.

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
OpenAPI is a specification that describes REST APIs in a machine-readable format.

FastAPI automatically generates an OpenAPI document based on your routes, models, parameters, and metadata.

This OpenAPI specification powers FastAPI's documentation tools.

docs.title: Swagger UI
docs.text:
Swagger UI provides an interactive web interface for exploring and testing APIs.

FastAPI automatically generates Swagger UI.

By default:

/docs

displays interactive API documentation.

Developers can:

  • Browse endpoints
  • View schemas
  • Submit requests
  • Inspect responses

without writing any additional code.

docs.title: ReDoc
docs.text:
ReDoc provides an alternative documentation interface.

By default:

/redoc

displays a more documentation-oriented view of the API.

Many teams prefer ReDoc for reading and exploration.

docs.title: Route Metadata
docs.text:
Route metadata improves generated documentation.

Examples:

@app.get(
    "/users",
    summary="List users",
    description="Retrieve all users"
)

This information appears automatically in generated documentation.

Metadata helps explain endpoint behavior.

docs.title: Request Models
docs.text:
Pydantic models contribute directly to generated documentation.

Example:

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: str

FastAPI automatically documents:

  • Fields
  • Types
  • Required values

Consumers can understand request expectations without separate documentation.

docs.title: Response Models
docs.text:
Response models describe endpoint outputs.

Example:

@app.get(
    "/users/{user_id}",
    response_model=User
)

FastAPI automatically includes the response structure in the documentation.

This makes API contracts visible and discoverable.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags organize related endpoints.

Example:

@app.get(
    "/users",
    tags=["Users"]
)

This groups endpoints within the documentation interface.

Tags improve navigation as APIs grow.

docs.title: Application Metadata
docs.text:
FastAPI allows API-wide metadata.

Example:

app = FastAPI(
    title="User API",
    description="Manage users",
    version="1.0.0"
)

This information appears throughout generated documentation.

In professional environments, documentation is often the primary way consumers discover and learn an API.

Understanding FastAPI's documentation features helps you build APIs that are easier to learn, easier to use, and easier to maintain over time.

docs.title: FastAPI Error Handling
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Error Handling capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • The problem error handling solves
  • Why error handling matters
  • General API engineering concepts behind error handling

Error Handling is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
FastAPI provides built-in tools for handling API failures in a consistent and predictable manner.

These tools make it easier to communicate errors clearly while minimizing boilerplate code.

Benefits include:

✅ Less boilerplate

✅ Consistent error responses

✅ Built-in HTTP status code support

✅ Automatic OpenAPI documentation

✅ Customizable exception handling

✅ Cleaner endpoint code

Instead of manually building error responses everywhere, FastAPI provides reusable mechanisms that help keep APIs maintainable.

docs.title: HTTPException
docs.text:
HTTPException is FastAPI's primary mechanism for returning API errors.

Example:

from fastapi import HTTPException

raise HTTPException(
    status_code=404,
    detail="User not found"
)

This automatically creates an appropriate error response.

docs.title: Status Codes
docs.text:
Status codes communicate the general category of a response.

Common examples:

200 OK
201 Created
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error

Choosing appropriate status codes helps API consumers understand what happened.

docs.title: detail
docs.text:
The detail parameter contains information about the error.

Example:

raise HTTPException(
    status_code=404,
    detail="Book not found"
)

Response:

{
  "detail": "Book not found"
}

The detail message should be clear and helpful.

docs.title: Custom Exceptions
docs.text:
As APIs grow, repeating the same HTTPException logic becomes tedious.

Custom exceptions allow reusable error definitions.

Example:

class UserNotFoundError(Exception):
    pass

These exceptions can later be handled centrally.

docs.title: Exception Handlers
docs.text:
Exception handlers define application-wide error behavior.

Example:

@app.exception_handler(UserNotFoundError)
async def user_not_found_handler(request, exc):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=404,
        content={
            "error": {
                "code": "USER_NOT_FOUND",
                "message": "User does not exist"
            }
        }
    )

Exception handlers help enforce consistency across an entire API.

docs.title: Validation Errors
docs.text:
FastAPI automatically validates request data.

If validation fails:

class User(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr

and the request contains invalid data, FastAPI automatically returns a validation error response.

This reduces the amount of error handling developers must write manually.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You encounter the following endpoint:

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/users/{user_id}")
def get_user(user_id: int):

    if user_id != 1:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=404,
            detail="User not found"
        )

    return {"id": 1, "name": "Jonas"}

developers can create APIs that communicate failures clearly and consistently.

In professional environments, error handling is essential because API consumers spend significant time diagnosing problems and recovering from failures.

Understanding FastAPI's error handling tools allows you to build APIs that are easier to maintain, easier to debug, and more enjoyable to use.

docs.title: FastAPI Filtering
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Filtering capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • The problem filtering solves
  • Why filtering matters
  • General API engineering concepts behind filtering

Filtering is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
FastAPI makes filtering straightforward because query parameters are automatically mapped to Python function parameters.

Benefits include:

✅ Minimal boilerplate

✅ Automatic request parsing

✅ Automatic validation

✅ Automatic type conversion

✅ Automatic OpenAPI documentation

✅ Clear and readable route definitions

Instead of manually extracting and validating values from requests, FastAPI handles much of the work automatically.

This allows API engineers to focus on designing useful filtering behavior rather than request-parsing logic.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Query parameters are the most common mechanism for implementing filtering.

Example:

GET /products?category=books

FastAPI automatically maps query parameters to function arguments.

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(category: str | None = None):
    ...

docs.title: Optional Parameters
docs.text:
Most filters should be optional.

Example:

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(category: str | None = None):
    ...

Requests can be:

GET /products

or:

GET /products?category=books

The same endpoint can support multiple filtering scenarios.

docs.title: Multiple Filters
docs.text:
Filtering often involves multiple query parameters.

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(
    category: str | None = None,
    status: str | None = None
):
    ...

Example request:

GET /products?category=books&status=active

FastAPI handles parameter extraction automatically.

docs.title: Type Conversion
docs.text:
FastAPI converts query parameters into Python types.

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(min_price: float | None = None):
    ...

Example:

GET /products?min_price=100

FastAPI converts:

"100"

into:

100.0

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
FastAPI validates query parameters using type annotations.

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(min_price: int):
    ...

If a consumer provides:

GET /products?min_price=abc

FastAPI automatically returns a validation error.

docs.title: Query()
docs.text:
FastAPI provides Query() for additional validation rules.

Example:

from fastapi import Query

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(
    limit: int = Query(10, ge=1, le=100)
):
    ...

This allows:

  • default values
  • minimum values
  • maximum values
  • descriptions

docs.text:

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/products")

docs.text:

You will encounter filtering in almost every professional API, including:

Understanding how FastAPI implements filtering is an important step toward becoming comfortable building data-discovery experiences in real-world APIs.

docs.title: FastAPI Pagination
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Pagination capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • The problem pagination solves
  • Why pagination matters
  • General API engineering concepts behind pagination

Pagination is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
FastAPI provides excellent support for pagination through query parameters, type validation, and automatic documentation.

Benefits include:

✅ Minimal boilerplate

✅ Automatic query parameter handling

✅ Automatic validation

✅ Automatic OpenAPI documentation

✅ Consistent request patterns

✅ Easy integration with filtering and sorting

Rather than manually parsing request values, FastAPI automatically converts and validates pagination inputs.

This allows API engineers to focus on API design rather than request-processing code.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Pagination is most commonly implemented using query parameters.

Example:

GET /products?page=1&page_size=20

FastAPI automatically maps these values to function parameters.

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(
    page: int = 1,
    page_size: int = 20
):
    ...

docs.title: Page Numbers
docs.text:
One common pagination strategy is page-based pagination.

Example:

GET /products?page=3&page_size=20

Conceptually:

Page 1 → Items 1-20

Page 2 → Items 21-40

Page 3 → Items 41-60

This approach is easy for consumers to understand.

docs.title: Limit and Offset
docs.text:
Another common strategy is limit/offset pagination.

Example:

GET /products?offset=40&limit=20

Meaning:

Skip first 40 items

Return next 20 items

FastAPI easily supports this pattern through query parameters.

docs.title: Query()
docs.text:
FastAPI provides Query() for pagination validation.

Example:

from fastapi import Query

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(
    page_size: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=100)
):
    ...

This helps prevent:

  • negative values
  • page sizes that are too large
  • invalid requests

docs.title: Pagination Metadata
docs.text:
Pagination is usually more useful when additional information is returned.

Example:

{
    "items": [...],
    "page": 2,
    "page_size": 20,
    "total_items": 250
}

FastAPI does not generate pagination metadata automatically.

API engineers typically create it themselves.

docs.title: Combining Pagination and Filtering
docs.text:
Pagination frequently works together with filtering.

Example:

GET /products?category=books&page=2

Consumers first narrow the data set.

Then they page through the results.

This combination is extremely common in professional APIs.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are given the following endpoint:

@app.get("/products")
def get_products(
    page: int = 1,
    page_size: int = 20
):
    return {
        "page": page,
        "page_size": page_size
    }

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand how FastAPI receives pagination inputs.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to explain:

  • where pagination values come from
  • how FastAPI converts request values
  • why default values are useful

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Look at the function parameters.

Stronger Hint

FastAPI automatically maps query parameters to Python arguments.

Almost There

Requests can override the default values.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

FastAPI treats page and page_size as query parameters.

Example:

GET /products?page=3&page_size=50

Produces:

page = 3
page_size = 50

FastAPI performs the conversion automatically.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: The goal is to understand how FastAPI receives pagination information from incoming requests.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You have the following endpoint:

@app.get("/products")
def get_products():
    return products

Consumers only want 20 products at a time.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Add basic pagination.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • accept page numbers
  • accept page sizes
  • return only a subset of results

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Use query parameters.

Stronger Hint

Calculate where the page starts.

Almost There

Slice the collection using the calculated values.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution 
@app.get("/products")
def get_products(
    page: int = 1,
    page_size: int = 20
):
    start = (page - 1) * page_size
    end = start + page_size

    return products[start:end]

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: The goal is to reinforce the basic mechanics of page-based pagination.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building an e-commerce API.

Consumers want:

  • category filtering
  • pagination
  • pagination metadata

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Create a complete paginated endpoint.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to combine:

  • filtering
  • pagination
  • response metadata

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Apply filtering first.

Stronger Hint

Pagination should operate on the filtered result set.

Almost There

Include helpful pagination information in the response.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution 
@app.get("/products")
def get_products(
    category: str | None = None,
    page: int = 1,
    page_size: int = 20
):
    results = products

    if category:
        results = [
            p for p in results
            if p["category"] == category
        ]

    total_items = len(results)

    start = (page - 1) * page_size
    end = start + page_size

    return {
        "items": results[start:end],
        "page": page,
        "page_size": page_size,
        "total_items": total_items,
    }

Real-world APIs often combine multiple capabilities.

docs.text: Professional FastAPI projects often standardize common patterns to improve maintainability and consistency.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: Pagination parameters are accepted but never applied.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text:

A consumer could request:

items.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: The focus remains solely on the data itself.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Return helpful information such as:

  • current page
  • page size
  • total item count

This improves consumer experience.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: Pagination logic is implemented before data-discovery logic.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Apply:

Filtering
    ↓
Sorting
    ↓
Pagination

This typically produces more useful results.

docs.text:
Different developers make different choices.

Examples:

page

current_page

p

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Establish shared conventions across the API.

Consistency is valuable.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Pagination is one of the most common capabilities implemented in modern APIs.

FastAPI makes pagination straightforward through:

  • query parameters
  • automatic type conversion
  • validation
  • OpenAPI documentation

These features allow API engineers to implement pagination with relatively little code while maintaining good API design practices.

You will encounter pagination in:

  • public APIs
  • internal APIs
  • e-commerce systems
  • reporting systems
  • data platforms
  • SaaS products

Understanding how FastAPI implements pagination is an important step toward building APIs that remain usable and scalable as datasets grow.

docs.title: FastAPI Routing
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Routing capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • What routing is
  • Why routing matters
  • Resources and endpoints
  • Path parameters
  • Query parameters
  • Route design principles

Routing is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why FastAPI Routing Is Powerful
docs.text:
FastAPI provides a clean and explicit way to define routes.

Instead of manually inspecting incoming requests and deciding what code should run, FastAPI maps requests directly to Python functions.

Benefits:

✅ Less boilerplate

✅ Readable code

✅ Automatic validation

✅ Automatic documentation

✅ Easy route organization

✅ Strong editor support

Routing is often one of the first FastAPI features developers encounter because nearly everything in an API begins with a route.

docs.title: Route Decorators
docs.text:
Route decorators connect URLs and HTTP methods to Python functions.

Examples:

@app.get("/books")

@app.post("/books")

@app.put("/books/{book_id}")

@app.delete("/books/{book_id}")

docs.title: Path Parameters
docs.text:
Path parameters allow routes to operate on specific resources.

Example:

@app.get("/books/{book_id}")

When a request arrives:

GET /books/123

FastAPI extracts:

book_id = 123

automatically.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Query parameters modify how a route behaves.

Example:

@app.get("/books")
def get_books(category: str):
    ...

Request:

GET /books?category=python

FastAPI automatically extracts:

category = "python"

docs.title: APIRouter
docs.text:
As APIs grow, placing every route in a single file becomes difficult to maintain.

FastAPI provides:

APIRouter

to organize related routes.

Example:

users_router

books_router

orders_router

This helps keep larger APIs maintainable.

Stronger Hint

GET /users/42

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

This route:

@app.get("/users/{user_id}")

responds to:

GET

requests.

The path parameter:

user_id

identifies which user should be returned.

Example:

GET /users/42

produces:

{
  "user_id": 42
}

docs.title: FastAPI Testing
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Testing capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • The problem testing solves
  • Why testing matters
  • General API engineering concepts behind testing

Testing is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
FastAPI provides excellent support for API testing.

Benefits include:

✅ Minimal setup

✅ Fast test execution

✅ Easy endpoint testing

✅ Automatic request simulation

✅ Better maintainability

✅ Greater confidence during refactoring

FastAPI makes it possible to test endpoints without running a real server.

This allows developers to verify API behavior quickly and repeatedly during development.

docs.title: TestClient
docs.text:
FastAPI provides the TestClient for sending requests to an application during testing.

Example:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

client = TestClient(app)

The client behaves similarly to a real API consumer.

docs.title: Test Functions
docs.text:
Tests are typically written as Python functions.

Example:

def test_health_check():
    ...

Each test focuses on a specific behavior.

docs.title: Sending Requests
docs.text:
The test client can send requests using common HTTP methods.

Examples:

client.get()

client.post()

client.put()

client.delete()

This allows developers to simulate consumer interactions.

docs.title: Response Assertions
docs.text:
Tests verify that responses match expectations.

Examples:

assert response.status_code == 200

assert response.json() == {...}

Assertions define what "correct behavior" means.

docs.title: Happy Path Testing
docs.text:
Happy path tests verify expected success scenarios.

Example:

Valid input
        ↓
Success response

These tests confirm that the API works when used correctly.

docs.title: Error Testing
docs.text:
Testing should also verify failure behavior.

Examples:

Invalid input

Missing fields

Unauthorized requests

Resource not found

Many bugs are discovered by testing these scenarios.

docs.title: Test Isolation
docs.text:
Good tests should not depend on the outcome of previous tests.

Each test should:

Set up its own data
        ↓
Execute behavior
        ↓
Verify results

This makes tests more reliable and easier to maintain.

docs.title: Automated Execution
docs.text:
Tests are designed to run repeatedly.

Example:

pytest

As the API evolves, the same tests can be executed many times to detect regressions.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are given the following test:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

client = TestClient(app)


def test_root():
    response = client.get("/")

    assert response.status_code == 200

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand how FastAPI tests API behavior.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to explain:

  • what the test client does
  • what the request is testing
  • what the assertion verifies

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Look at the call to client.get().

Stronger Hint

The test behaves like an API consumer.

Almost There

The assertion verifies that the endpoint returns a successful response.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

The test client sends a GET request to the root endpoint.

The assertion checks that the endpoint returns HTTP 200.

If the endpoint returns a different status code, the test fails.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: The goal is to understand the basic structure of a FastAPI test before creating more complex tests.

docs.text:

@app.get("/health")
def health():

docs.text: Write a test that verifies the endpoint works correctly.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Use client.get().

Stronger Hint

Check both the status code and returned JSON.

Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: The goal is to reinforce the basic workflow of sending requests and verifying responses.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building an API with:

  • validation
  • authentication
  • pagination

A products endpoint requires:

  • authentication
  • valid query parameters

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Create a testing strategy for multiple API capabilities.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to combine:

  • endpoint testing
  • validation testing
  • authorization testing

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think beyond successful requests.

Stronger Hint

What happens when authentication is missing?

Almost There

A complete test suite verifies both valid and invalid scenarios.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

A reasonable test suite might verify:

Authenticated request succeeds

Unauthenticated request fails

Valid pagination works

Invalid pagination returns validation errors

Expected response structure is returned

Rather than testing only successful requests, the suite verifies important behaviors throughout the endpoint lifecycle.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Real-world APIs depend on multiple capabilities interacting correctly.

Testing should reflect how APIs are actually used.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your organization has many APIs.

Teams repeatedly create identical setup code:

client = TestClient(app)

Database preparation code is duplicated.

Authentication helpers are copied between projects.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Create reusable testing patterns.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • identify duplication
  • create reusable solutions
  • standardize implementation patterns

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Look for repeated code across test files.

Stronger Hint

Shared fixtures can reduce duplication.

Almost There

Consistent testing patterns improve maintainability.

docs.title: Solution
Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Professional FastAPI applications often depend on reusable testing patterns that keep test suites organized and maintainable as projects grow.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: Developers focus only on successful requests.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Test both successful and failure scenarios.

Include:

  • invalid input
  • missing authentication
  • resource not found
  • validation errors

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: A single test verifies many unrelated behaviors.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Keep tests focused on one behavior whenever possible.

Smaller tests are easier to understand and debug.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: Developers only verify HTTP 200 responses.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Verify expected failure behavior as well.

Professional APIs must handle errors correctly.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: Tests depend on data created by previous tests.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Make tests independent and repeatable.

Each test should establish its own assumptions.

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: Tests exist but are rarely executed.

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Run tests frequently during development.

The value of automated testing comes from continuous validation.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Testing is one of the most important implementation skills for FastAPI developers.

FastAPI makes testing straightforward through:

  • TestClient
  • request simulation
  • response assertions
  • integration with pytest

These tools allow developers to verify API behavior quickly and consistently.

You will use API testing in:

  • feature development
  • bug fixing
  • refactoring
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • production-quality applications

Understanding how FastAPI implements testing is essential for building APIs that can evolve safely and confidently over time.

docs.text:

  • why testing exists

  • testing strategies
  • API quality principles

docs.title: FastAPI Validation
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the validation concepts introduced in the Validation capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • Why validation exists
  • Common validation rules
  • Request validation
  • Response validation

Validation is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why FastAPI Validation Is Powerful
docs.text:
FastAPI provides built-in validation through Pydantic.

Instead of manually checking values:

if not email:
    ...

or:

if age < 0:
    ...

you define the expected structure of your data and FastAPI automatically validates incoming requests.

Benefits:

✅ Less boilerplate

✅ Consistent validation

✅ Automatic documentation

✅ Useful error messages

✅ Easier maintenance

docs.title: Request Validation
docs.text:
A common use case is validating incoming request data.

Imagine a user registration endpoint.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    age: int


@app.post("/users")
def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    return user

FastAPI automatically validates:

  • Required fields
  • Data types
  • Request structure

If validation fails, FastAPI returns an error response.

docs.title: Missing Required Fields
docs.text:
Suppose a client sends:

{
  "email": "jonas@example.com"
}

The request is missing:

username

FastAPI automatically returns an error.

You do not need to write custom validation code for required fields.

docs.title: Type Validation
docs.text:
Suppose a client sends:

{
  "username": "jonas",
  "email": "jonas@example.com",
  "age": "twenty-five"
}

FastAPI expects:

age: int

Validation fails before the endpoint logic runs.

This prevents invalid data from entering the application.

docs.title: Adding Validation Rules
docs.text:
Many APIs require stronger validation than simple type checking.

Pydantic's Field() can be used to specify validation rules.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(
        min_length=3,
        max_length=50
    )

    age: int = Field(
        gt=0,
        lt=120
    )

Examples:

min_length
max_length
gt (greater than)
lt (less than)
ge (greater than or equal)
le (less than or equal)

These rules are automatically enforced.

docs.title: Email Validation
docs.text:
Many APIs accept email addresses.

Pydantic provides specialized types.

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr

Now FastAPI validates that incoming values look like valid email addresses.

Example:

✅ jonas@example.com

❌ not-an-email

docs.title: Response Validation
docs.text:
FastAPI can also validate data leaving the API.

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str
    email: str

@app.get("/users/{user_id}",
         response_model=UserResponse)
def get_user(user_id: int):
    return {
        "id": user_id,
        "username": "jonas",
        "email": "jonas@example.com"
    }

Benefits:

  • Consistent responses
  • Better API contracts
  • Safer refactoring
  • Improved documentation

docs.title: Custom Validation
docs.text:
Sometimes business rules require custom validation.

Example:

Usernames cannot contain spaces.

Pydantic allows custom validators.

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str

    @field_validator("username")
    @classmethod
    def validate_username(cls, value):
        if " " in value:
            raise ValueError(
                "Username cannot contain spaces."
            )

        return value

This automatically runs whenever a request is validated.

docs.title: Validation Errors
docs.text:
When validation fails, FastAPI automatically returns structured error responses.

Example:

{
  "detail": [
    {
      "type": "string_too_short",
      "loc": ["body", "username"],
      "msg": "String should have at least 3 characters"
    }
  ]
}

This makes it easier for API consumers to understand what went wrong.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A colleague has created the following API model:

from pydantic import BaseModel

class ProductCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float

You need to understand what FastAPI will validate automatically.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify the automatic validation behaviour.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
You should be able to explain:

  • which fields are required
  • which types are expected
  • what happens if validation fails

Hints

Small Hint

Look at each field definition.

Stronger Hint

Every field has a Python type.

Almost There

FastAPI uses these type hints to validate incoming data.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

FastAPI validates:

  • name is required
  • price is required
  • name must be a string
  • price must be a float

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Before creating validation rules yourself, you should understand the validation FastAPI already provides automatically.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a product API.

A product name should:

  • contain at least 3 characters
  • contain no more than 100 characters

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Add validation rules to the model.

Starting point:

from pydantic import BaseModel

class ProductCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The API should reject:

  • names shorter than 3 characters
  • names longer than 100 characters

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Look at Pydantic's Field() helper.

Stronger Hint

Field can define minimum and maximum lengths.

Almost There

Investigate:

Field(min_length=?, max_length=?)

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution 
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class ProductCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(
        min_length=3,
        max_length=100
    )

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Most validation work involves extending the basic validation FastAPI already provides.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are creating a blog API.

Each blog post contains:

  • title
  • content
  • author_email

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Create a model that validates:

  • title length
  • content length
  • email format

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your solution should use:

  • Field()
  • EmailStr
  • sensible validation limits

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

You'll need more than one validation technique.

Stronger Hint

Think about both field constraints and specialized types.

Almost There

EmailStr handles email validation automatically.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

    BaseModel,
    EmailStr,
    Field
)


class BlogPostCreate(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(
        min_length=5,
        max_length=200
    )

    content: str = Field(
        min_length=50
    )

    author_email: EmailStr

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Real APIs rarely validate only one field. Most models combine multiple validation techniques.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your organization maintains:

  • User APIs
  • Product APIs
  • Billing APIs
  • Reporting APIs

Many models use:

  • email addresses
  • timestamps
  • pagination parameters

You notice the same validation rules appearing repeatedly.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Identify reusable validation patterns.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Design:

  • at least one reusable model
  • at least one reusable validation approach

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Think about models shared across multiple endpoints.

Stronger Hint

Pagination often uses the same fields repeatedly.

Almost There

Common concepts such as email addresses and pagination can often be standardized.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

Example:

class PaginationParams(BaseModel):
    page: int = 1
    page_size: int = 25

This model can be reused across multiple endpoints.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: As APIs grow, reusable validation patterns improve consistency and reduce duplication.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
FastAPI's validation features allow developers to focus on defining API contracts rather than writing repetitive validation logic.

As systems grow, strong validation becomes increasingly important for:

  • Reliability
  • Security
  • Maintainability
  • API usability

The goal is not simply to learn Pydantic or FastAPI syntax.

The goal is to understand how FastAPI helps implement one of the most important API Engineering capabilities:

Validation

docs.title: FastAPI Versioning
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how FastAPI implements the concepts introduced in the Versioning capability page.

Before reading this page, it is recommended that you first understand:

  • The problem versioning solves
  • Why versioning matters
  • General API engineering concepts behind versioning

Versioning is a capability.

FastAPI is one way of implementing that capability.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
FastAPI provides several straightforward approaches for API versioning.

Benefits include:

✅ Clear route organization

✅ Easy support for multiple API versions

✅ Automatic OpenAPI documentation

✅ Gradual migration paths

✅ Reduced risk of breaking consumers

✅ Good maintainability as APIs evolve

FastAPI does not enforce a specific versioning strategy.

Instead, it provides flexible routing and dependency features that allow API engineers to choose an appropriate approach.

docs.title: Path Versioning
docs.text:
The most common FastAPI versioning approach is path versioning.

Example:

/api/v1/products

/api/v2/products

FastAPI routes can easily support multiple versions:

@app.get("/api/v1/products")
def get_products_v1():
    ...


@app.get("/api/v2/products")
def get_products_v2():
    ...

This approach is explicit and easy for consumers to understand.

docs.title: APIRouter
docs.text:
FastAPI's APIRouter helps organize versioned endpoints.

Example:

from fastapi import APIRouter

v1_router = APIRouter(
    prefix="/api/v1"
)

v2_router = APIRouter(
    prefix="/api/v2"
)

This allows related endpoints to be grouped together.

docs.title: Multiple Endpoint Versions
docs.text:
Different API versions often coexist.

Example:

Version 1
    ↓
Legacy consumers

Version 2
    ↓
New consumers

FastAPI allows multiple route implementations to exist simultaneously.

docs.title: Shared Business Logic
docs.text:
Versioned APIs often share underlying business logic.

Example:

def get_products():
    ...

Version-specific routes can call shared functions.

This reduces duplication while preserving version-specific behavior.

docs.title: Response Evolution
docs.text:
One of the most common versioning scenarios involves response changes.

Version 1:

{
  "name": "Jane Doe"
}

Version 2:

{
  "first_name": "Jane",
  "last_name": "Doe"
}

FastAPI allows separate endpoints and response models for each version.

docs.title: Response Models
docs.text:
Versioned APIs frequently use different response models.

Example:

class UserV1(BaseModel):
    name: str


class UserV2(BaseModel):
    first_name: str
    last_name: str

This helps clearly separate behavior between versions.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
FastAPI automatically generates OpenAPI documentation.

Versioned routes appear as separate endpoints.

This helps consumers understand available versions and migration paths.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are given the following FastAPI application:

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/api/v1/products")
def get_products_v1():
    return {
        "version": "v1"
    }


@app.get("/api/v2/products")
def get_products_v2():
    return {
        "version": "v2"
    }

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Understand how FastAPI supports API versioning.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to explain:

  • how FastAPI distinguishes versions
  • why multiple routes can exist
  • which version a request will receive

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Look carefully at the route paths.

Stronger Hint

The version appears in the URL.

Almost There

Requests to different URLs reach different route handlers.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Solution

FastAPI treats each version as a separate route.

Request:

GET /api/v1/products

Returns Version 1.

Request:

GET /api/v2/products

Returns Version 2.

Each route can evolve independently.

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: The goal is to understand the most common versioning approach used in FastAPI applications.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You currently have:

@app.get("/products")
def get_products():
    ...

A breaking change is required.

The old behavior must continue working.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Create a versioned endpoint.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
The learner should be able to:

  • introduce a new API version
  • preserve the existing version
  • organize routes clearly

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Small Hint

Existing consumers should not break.

Stronger Hint

Create separate routes for each version.

Almost There

Use version-specific URL paths.

docs.title: Solution
Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: The goal is to reinforce the core implementation pattern of introducing a new version without disrupting existing consumers.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a customer management API.

Version 1 returns:

{
  "name": "Jane Doe"
}

Version 2 should return:

{
  "first_name": "Jane",
  "last_name": "Doe"

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Versioning is one of the most important capabilities for long-lived APIs.

FastAPI makes versioning relatively straightforward through:

  • path-based routing
  • APIRouter organization
  • response models
  • automatic documentation

These features make it easier to support API evolution while reducing the risk of breaking existing consumers.

You will encounter API versioning in:

  • public APIs
  • SaaS platforms
  • enterprise systems
  • internal service ecosystems
  • third-party integration platforms

Understanding how FastAPI implements versioning is an important step toward building APIs that can evolve safely over time.
